vignette: The seizure strikes on a quiet Tuesday in March. Arjun is ten when his body locks on the sidewalk, when the taxi screeches to a halt, when she spends three weeks in a pediatric ICU chair that bites into her lower back. The monitors beep like metronomes counting down. She counts every breath, every shift in his chest, learning early that time is not linear when your child's lungs refuse to expand. When he finally turns green and comes home, she carries the ICU's hum under her skin. The recovery takes years, and the shop opens in the quiet aftermath. At fifty-seven, she runs the grocer herself, weighing lemongrass, checking expiry dates on coconut milk, stacking crates of morning glory with deliberate care. The narrow aisles become a perimeter. She opens at six, always checks the gas line twice, and runs her palm along the doorframe where Arjun used to leave height marks. When the night delivery truck backs up, her stomach drops before she even hears the engine. She maps every aisle in her head, noting sightlines, water bottles, the nearest wall phone. Safety, she decides, is a geometry. The distress arrives in increments, never with warning. A sudden cough from a customer three shelves over makes her count her own breaths until the rhythm steadies. She no longer drives to the hospital for Arjun's annual checkups; she has him drive, her knuckles white on the dashboard, her eyes fixed on the rearview mirror where she still sometimes sees the white sheets and the IV pole. She stops going to the neighborhood clinic altogether. The waiting room chairs, the antiseptic smell, the low murmur of worried parents-it all folds back into her bones like wet paper. She cancels the monthly family dinner when the menu shifts to grilled meats, suddenly unable to bear the smoke alarm's test chirp. Her husband, David, watches her from the threshold of their bedroom, his questions hanging in the air like dust. "You don't have to carry it all," he says. She nods, but the silence between them has widened into something she does not know how to cross. She loves him fiercely, but the love has grown careful, measured in small concessions and avoided conversations. She flinches when Arjun twists his ankle walking into the kitchen. She stops leaving windows cracked at night. She drinks ginger tea only when it is still hot, afraid to watch it cool. Tonight, the shop is closed. The fluorescent lights hum off. She stands at the counter, wiping it down in slow, even strokes. A delivery receipt lies beneath her palm. She traces the numbers until they blur. Outside, a siren wails, distant and fading. She does not freeze. She does not run. She simply rests her forehead against the cool glass of the front window, watches the streetlights reflect on the wet pavement, and waits for her breathing to return to its ordinary pace.
